chunks: And the Sheikh, may God support him, informed me of it. He said: Ahmad ibn Muhammad informed me, from his father, from Muhammad ibn al-Hasan al-Saffar, from Ahmad ibn Muhammad ibn 'Isa and al-Husayn ibn al-Hasan ibn Aban — both together — from al-Husayn ibn Sa'id, from Hammad, from Hariz, from whoever informed him, from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him):
Concerning a man from whom vermin fall while he is in salat — he said: 'He continues in his salat, and that does not nullify his wudu.'

key_terms.الدَّوَابُّ: vermin, insects, crawling creatures — lice, fleas, or similar parasites that may fall from a person's body
key_terms.وُضُوءَهُ: his wudu (ablution) — the minor ritual purification required for valid salat
key_terms.يَمْضِي: he continues, proceeds — instruction to complete the prayer without interruption
key_terms.يَنْقُضُ: nullifies, breaks, invalidates — the technical fiqh term for actions that break wudu

ai.seo_question: Does dropping or losing insects from one's body during salat break wudu or require restarting the prayer in Shia fiqh?
ai.summary: This hadith records a jurisprudential ruling from Imam Ja'far al-Sadiq (peace be upon him) regarding a man from whose body insects or crawling creatures fall during salat. The Imam rules that such an involuntary occurrence neither interrupts nor invalidates the salat, nor does it nullify the wudu. This establishes that only the specific legally-defined nullifiers of taharah break wudu, and incidental bodily occurrences of this nature are not among them.
